This loop is where all the learning happens. Each pass finds the single most common pair of neighbouring
and glues that pair together everywhere at once. It is greedy (it always takes the top pair), global
(it looks at every word at once) and deterministic: running it twice on the same
same order. The order matters, because

An unknown word costs positions, not meaning
— "q" + "u" + "o" + "k" + "k" + "a</w>". Nothing later on notices or complains: the sentence is simply
longer than it would be for a
known word. Each piece gets its own embedding, its own position and its own row in the attention tables, and the model has to work out from context that they
belong together. That is the whole case for subword tokenization — the
stays a fixed size, no input is ever impossible to represent, and a rare word
costs a few extra positions instead of being lost. In this tiny
"k" and "q" are not even known as single letters, so they become
